name: Foundations
short_definition: The programming, mathematics and data skills that everything else assumes. You do not need all of it before starting machine learning, but gaps here surface later as confusion.

name: Python for AI/ML
short_definition: Writing clear Python and using the numerical stack: arrays, dataframes, notebooks, environments and packaging. The practical entry point for almost every other topic here.

name: Linear algebra
short_definition: Vectors, matrices, projections and decompositions. It is the language models are written in: an embedding is a vector and a layer is a matrix multiply.

name: Calculus for ML
short_definition: Derivatives, gradients and the chain rule, aimed squarely at understanding how training works. Enough to read an optimiser, not a full analysis course.

name: Probability and statistics
short_definition: Distributions, expectation, estimation, uncertainty and hypothesis testing. This is what separates a real result from a number that happened once.

name: Data handling and visualisation
short_definition: Loading, cleaning, reshaping, joining and plotting data. In practice this is where most of the time on any real project actually goes.

name: Algorithms and computational thinking
short_definition: Complexity, data structures and decomposing a problem into steps a machine can execute. Matters most when your code has to run over data that no longer fits in memory.

name: Machine Learning
short_definition: Learning patterns from data to make predictions or find structure, using models simple enough that you can usually see why they behaved the way they did.

name: Supervised learning
short_definition: Learning a mapping from inputs to known labels. The setting behind most deployed machine learning, and the one where evaluation is best understood.

name: Unsupervised learning
short_definition: Finding structure in data with no labels: grouping, compressing, and describing what a dataset contains. Powerful, but much harder to evaluate honestly.

name: Semi- and self-supervised learning
short_definition: Getting a training signal from unlabelled data, either by using a little labelled data alongside a lot of unlabelled data, or by inventing a task the data can answer itself.

name: Regression and classification
short_definition: Predicting a number versus predicting a category. Different loss functions, different metrics, and different ways of being wrong.

name: Trees and ensembles
short_definition: Decision trees, random forests and gradient boosting. Still the strongest default for tabular data, and often better than a neural network on it.

name: Clustering and dimensionality reduction
short_definition: Grouping similar records and projecting high-dimensional data down to something you can plot or model. Easy to run, easy to over-interpret.

name: Feature engineering
short_definition: Turning raw records into inputs a model can use: encoding, scaling, aggregating and deriving. Often a bigger lever on accuracy than the choice of model.

name: Model selection and validation
short_definition: Splitting data, cross-validating, tuning and comparing models without fooling yourself. The discipline that decides whether your reported number means anything.

name: Interpretability
short_definition: Explaining what a model learned and why it made a given prediction, through inherently readable models or post-hoc attribution methods.

name: Responsible ML
short_definition: Fairness, harm, consent, transparency and the limits of what a model should be used to decide. A design concern from the first data collection, not a review at the end.

name: Deep Learning
short_definition: Neural networks with many layers, trained end to end by gradient descent. Buys enormous flexibility at the cost of data, compute and interpretability.

name: Neural-network fundamentals
short_definition: Layers, activations, losses and the forward pass. The smallest set of ideas that makes every later architecture legible rather than magical.

name: Optimisation and backpropagation
short_definition: How gradients are computed and applied: the chain rule at scale, plus learning rates, momentum and the practical business of making training converge.

name: CNNs and computer vision basics
short_definition: Convolutional architectures and the vision tasks that shaped them. Worth understanding even for NLP work, because so much transferable practice originated here.

name: Sequence modelling
short_definition: Handling inputs where order matters and length varies. The problem statement that attention and transformers were invented to answer.

name: Attention
short_definition: Letting a model weigh which parts of its input matter for each output position, instead of squeezing everything through one fixed-size state.

name: Transformers
short_definition: The architecture built around self-attention that now underpins most language, vision and multimodal models. Understanding it once explains a great deal.

name: Transfer learning
short_definition: Reusing a model trained on one task as the starting point for another. The reason useful results are reachable without a research budget.

name: Fine-tuning
short_definition: Continuing training on your own data to specialise a pretrained model, and knowing when a prompt or a retrieval step would have been sufficient instead.

name: Distributed and efficient training
short_definition: Mixed precision, gradient accumulation, sharding and multi-device training: the techniques that make large models trainable on the hardware you actually have.

name: Natural Language Processing
short_definition: Getting computers to work with human language: representing it, modelling it, retrieving from it, generating it, and evaluating whether any of that worked.

name: Text preprocessing and tokenisation
short_definition: Turning raw text into the discrete units a model consumes: normalisation, segmentation and subword vocabularies. The first place a mental model of an LLM usually breaks.

name: Representations and embeddings
short_definition: Mapping tokens, sentences or documents into vectors where geometric closeness reflects meaning. The substrate underneath search, clustering and retrieval.

name: Language modelling
short_definition: Learning the probability of text, usually by predicting the next token. The training objective behind essentially every modern generative language model.

name: RNNs and sequence-to-sequence models
short_definition: The recurrent and encoder-decoder designs that preceded transformers. Still the clearest way to see why attention was needed at all.

name: Transformers for NLP
short_definition: Applying transformer architectures to language: encoder, decoder and encoder-decoder variants, and which family suits which task.

name: Information retrieval
short_definition: Finding the documents that answer a query, from inverted indexes and BM25 through to learned rankers. Older than modern NLP and still indispensable.

name: Semantic search
short_definition: Retrieval by meaning rather than by exact words, using embeddings and vector indexes, usually combined with keyword search rather than replacing it.

name: Question answering
short_definition: Returning an answer rather than a list of documents, either by extracting a span from a passage or by generating one from retrieved context.

name: Text classification
short_definition: Assigning labels to text: topic, sentiment, intent, routing. The most common NLP task in production, and the best first project.

name: Summarisation and generation
short_definition: Producing new text conditioned on input. Easy to demo and genuinely hard to evaluate, because many different outputs can be equally correct.

name: NER and information extraction
short_definition: Pulling structured records out of unstructured text: entities, relations and attributes. Where language models meet databases.

name: Multilingual and low-resource NLP
short_definition: Working in languages with little training data or tooling. A reminder that benchmark results in English do not describe most of the world's languages.

name: NLP evaluation and safety
short_definition: Measuring whether a language system is actually good, and what it does when it fails: metrics, human evaluation, bias, and harmful output.

name: Generative AI and LLM applications
short_definition: Building useful software on top of large language models you did not train: prompting, retrieval, tools, evaluation, guardrails and the economics of running it.

name: Prompt design
short_definition: Specifying a task to a model precisely enough to get reliable results: instructions, examples, formatting and knowing which failures a prompt cannot fix.

name: Structured outputs
short_definition: Getting machine-readable results out of a text model — schemas, constrained decoding and validation — so the rest of your program can rely on the shape.

name: Retrieval-augmented generation
short_definition: Grounding a model's answers in documents you retrieve at query time. Mostly a retrieval and evaluation problem wearing a generation costume.

name: Tool use and agents
short_definition: Letting a model call functions, and letting it decide the sequence. Adds real capability and a great deal of failure surface at the same time.

name: Context management
short_definition: Deciding what goes into a limited context window and what gets summarised, cached or dropped. A systems-design problem, not a prompting trick.

name: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning
short_definition: Adapting a large model by training a small number of extra parameters. Usually the last thing to reach for, after prompting and retrieval have been ruled out.

name: LLM evaluation
short_definition: Deciding whether a change made the system better, using task-specific datasets, graders and human review rather than impressions from a handful of prompts.

name: Guardrails and safety
short_definition: Constraining what a deployed system will say and do: input and output filtering, injection resistance, refusal behaviour and escalation paths.

name: Cost, latency and reliability
short_definition: Making an LLM feature affordable and dependable: caching, batching, model choice, streaming, timeouts and graceful degradation.

name: Production architecture
short_definition: How the pieces fit together in a real system: retrieval, orchestration, state, observability and the boundaries between deterministic and probabilistic code.

name: Production AI and MLOps
short_definition: Everything between a working notebook and a system other people depend on: pipelines, packaging, deployment, monitoring, versioning and governance.

name: Data and feature pipelines
short_definition: Moving data reliably and computing the same features at training time and serving time. Skew between those two is a leading cause of silent failure.

name: Experiment tracking
short_definition: Recording what you ran, on what data, with which parameters and what came out — so a result can be found again months later and trusted.

name: Model packaging
short_definition: Turning a trained artefact into something reproducibly loadable elsewhere: serialisation formats, dependencies, and the interface around the weights.

name: Deployment and serving
short_definition: Running inference behind an interface others can call, with attention to batching, concurrency, hardware, cold starts and rollout strategy.

name: Monitoring and drift
short_definition: Noticing when a deployed model degrades because the world moved, not because the code changed. Requires measuring inputs and outcomes, not just uptime.

name: Data and model versioning
short_definition: Knowing exactly which data and which weights produced a given prediction, and being able to roll back either one independently.

name: Testing AI systems
short_definition: Testing components whose output is not deterministic: fixtures, tolerances, behavioural suites, regression sets and where ordinary unit tests still apply.

name: Security and privacy
short_definition: Protecting training data, model artefacts and user inputs: access control, PII handling, memorisation risk, prompt injection and supply-chain concerns.

name: Governance and compliance
short_definition: Documentation, approval, audit and accountability for automated decisions — including deciding that some decisions should not be automated at all.
